- If sentiment is negative or trending down, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift downward by 2–5%.
- If sentiment is positive and prices are rising, model often overshoots early in the horizon; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent peak or adjust downward after 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is flat or neutral, model frequently underestimates volatility; add 1–3% buffer to forecast for mean reversion or sudden spikes.
- If recent history shows sharp declines followed by recovery, model often fails to capture the rebound; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% after 3–5 days of low sentiment.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome exceeds model by >5% in first 5 days, reduce forecast slope for remaining days to avoid overcorrection.
- If sentiment history includes multiple negative values, model tends to underestimate true price; add 2–4% upward bias to forecast, especially if sentiment recovers.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp upward movement, consider sentiment shift as trigger for early upward correction.
- If sentiment is positive but model forecast is below recent low, model may be underestimating momentum; increase forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days if sentiment remains positive.
